name: Nikhil Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Nikhil, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, that works. I spend my days telling clients what's confidential, so it's nice to be on the other side.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day? What you do, what you like, and what wears you out.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I head the employment team at Hale Brennan, a small firm in a port town, and I act for workers: unfair dismissal, discrimination, unpaid wages. A lot of my clients come through the dockworkers' union branch, so my mornings are often calls with the branch rep about who got sacked this week. I like the tribunal days, when you finally put an employer's manager in the witness box. What wears me out is the bundles, hundreds of pages of emails and rotas I have to read before every hearing, and the pay, which is low for a lawyer because workers can't pay much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a useful tool and nothing more. I use it now and then to summarise a long email chain, and that's about the level it would stay at. I'd tell the union branch that their jobs aren't about to vanish, which is good news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but my money worries don't go anywhere. I've got about two weeks of savings because I pay part of my little sister's university rent, and the car loan eats the rest. Hale Brennan is the only firm doing worker-side employment law within an hour, so if anything happened there I'd have nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep using the summary tool for the bundles when I'm short of time. I'd ask Ruth Hale, the senior partner, whether we can take more no-win-no-fee cases, because those pay better when we win. I'd try to put a hundred a month aside once my sister finishes her degree next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a low hum of worry about money. It's the same hum I've had since I qualified. A plateau doesn't make it louder or quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pay is low. How do things work at home with your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam, my partner, is a paramedic, so we split the rent and he covers more of the food. It works, but neither of us has any slack. If his ambulance station changed shifts again, we'd feel it the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job you'd want AI to take, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bundles, definitely. If it could read four hundred pages of rotas and tell me where the manager changed his story, I'd buy it a drink. Just don't let it near the client meetings, because people who've been sacked need a human being.

say: AI is a **useful tool** and nothing more, at least for now.
The **union members** I represent aren't about to see their jobs vanish.
think: I'd be relieved, but I have only **two weeks** of savings.
Hale Brennan is the **only firm** doing worker-side employment law within an hour.
do: Keep using the **summary tool** for long bundles when short of time.
Ask the senior partner to take more **no-win-no-fee** cases.
Start saving **a hundred a month** once his sister graduates next summer.
feel: Mostly fine, with a **low hum** of money worry that never goes away.
S0.quote: People who've been sacked need a human being, so don't let AI near the client meetings.
fieldNote: He uses AI **only for reading**, and keeps it away from clients by choice.
His money is **stretched by family**: his sister's rent and a car loan.
His household has **no slack**, though his partner's pay steadies things.

steps.text: Keep using the summary tool on long tribunal bundles
Ask Ruth Hale to take more no-win-no-fee cases
Save a hundred a month once his sister graduates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say employers must not use AI as cover to sack people without proper consultation. I'd be writing that in the union newsletter and posting it everywhere. I'd also say workers need a seat at the table when these tools come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my own job is half reading and writing, so the software would eat into it. The firm would expect me to run more cases with less help, and I already work until nine some nights. I'm good at this, but I'm not sure being good protects you when the work itself gets cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the firm's legal research tool properly this year, once I'd seen it actually work on a real case. I'd offer the union branch training sessions on workers' rights when AI is brought in. I'd keep the car loan payments going and stop the takeaways to save a bit faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit torn. I like the idea of the dull parts going, but I don't like who gets to decide what the dull parts are. It's usually not the people doing the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't more workers being let go mean more work for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, yes, and that's the strange bit. There'd be a wave of dismissal claims, and I'd be busier than ever. But if the software is doing my drafting, Ruth won't need three lawyers to handle that wave, she'll need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which colleague at Hale Brennan would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, our paralegal. She prepares all the bundles, and that's the first thing the software does well. I'd want the firm to retrain her rather than let her go, and I'd say so to Ruth's face.

say: Employers must not use AI as **cover to sack** people without consultation.
Workers need a **seat at the table** when these tools come in.
think: Half my job is **reading and writing**, so the software would eat into it.
A wave of claims might need **one lawyer**, not three.
do: Learn the firm's **legal research tool** once it's proven on a real case.
Run **training sessions** for the union branch on workers' rights and AI.
Stop **takeaways** to save a little faster.
feel: **Uneasy and torn**, liking less drudgery but distrusting who decides.
S1.quote: There'd be a wave of dismissal claims, and I'd be busier than ever. But if the software is doing my drafting, the firm won't need three lawyers for that wave.
fieldNote: He sees a **short-term boom** in claims that wouldn't save lawyers' jobs.
He'd **adopt tools** once proven, but wants workers to have a say.
He worries most about the **paralegal**, whose bundle work goes first.

steps.text: Learn the firm's legal research tool on a live case
Run workers' rights training sessions for the dockworkers' union branch
Stop takeaways and put the difference into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a political answer, not a market one. Governments need to tax the companies that own these systems and fund an income for the people they replace. I'd be at union meetings saying we need to move now, because two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job as I know it ends around 2028. Every thinking part of employment law, the reading, the drafting, the advice, is exactly what this does. The only bit that might last is standing in a tribunal, and only if the rules insist on a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union's political campaign on day one and push for a tax on AI firms. I'd stop sending money for my sister's rent and ask my parents to cover it, which would be a horrible phone call. I'd think hard about retraining for something Sam does, something with your hands that robots don't reach until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I spent seven years getting here, and it's two years from the end. And I don't have the savings to take a breath and think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me three years, maybe, if I switched to something hands-on. Sam says ambulance crews will be needed after the AI arrives, because nobody's built a robot that can lift a patient down three flights of stairs yet. Retraining as a paramedic at twenty-eight would be a big pay cut, but it might be the only door open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sam talk about the night this was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit on the kitchen floor like we did when he failed his first driving assessment. Sam would say we've survived on less before. I'd say we haven't survived on nothing.

say: AGI needs a **political answer**: tax the owners and fund the people replaced.
With only **two years**, unions must move now.
think: My job as I know it **ends around 2028**.
Only **tribunal advocacy** might last, and only if the rules demand a person.
do: Join the union's **political campaign** for a tax on AI firms.
Ask his parents to take over his **sister's rent**.
Look into **retraining as a paramedic** before robots arrive.
feel: **Sick** at being two years from the end of a seven-year climb.
S2.quote: Nobody's built a robot that can lift a patient down three flights of stairs yet.
fieldNote: He sees the **robot delay** as a reason to move into hands-on work.
His partner's **paramedic job** makes that path feel real, not abstract.
Lack of **savings** takes away his time to think things through.

steps.text: Join the union campaign for a tax on AI companies
Ask his parents to take over his sister's university rent
Apply for a paramedic course at the local university

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to put rules in place: consultation, retraining money, and some income support for people who are pushed out. I'd say it calmly, because people listen to calm. I'd want my union clients to hear it from me first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I could ride the wave of AI dismissal claims for a few years and build some savings. That's grim, making money from other people's bad news, but that's what employment lawyers do. By 2031, I'd want to be out or in a role that a person is required to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools at work properly from the start, so I'm the fastest lawyer in the firm while lawyers still exist. I'd save every bonus from the claims wave, aiming for six months of costs by 2029. I'd start the part-time paramedic science course in year three, with Sam's help on the study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a plan, and a plan helps. It's still the same ending. I'd just be walking towards it rather than falling into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with five years compared to two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies and the governments who let them move this fast without any rules. Not the workers, and not even most of the bosses, who'd be scared too. I'd want that said clearly at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would be thrilled I was thinking of joining his world, though he'd warn me about the night shifts. He says I'd be good at keeping people calm, because that's what I do in tribunals. I'm not sure about the blood, though.

say: We have **five years** for rules on consultation, retraining and **income support**.
My **union clients** should hear it from me first.
think: I could ride the **claims wave** for a few years and build savings.
By **2031** I'd want to be out, or in a role needing a person.
do: Use the AI tools **from the start** to be the fastest lawyer in the firm.
Save every **bonus** from the claims wave, aiming for **six months** by 2029.
Start a **part-time paramedic** course in year three.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadier for having a plan.
S3.quote: With five years I'd be walking towards the end of my legal career rather than falling into it.
fieldNote: He admits the **claims wave** would profit from others' job losses.
He blames **tech firms and governments**, not workers or most bosses.
His partner's world offers a **second career** he takes seriously.

steps.text: Use the firm's AI tools daily from the first month
Bank every bonus from the claims wave, aiming for six months' costs
Start a part-time paramedic science course in year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, if governments actually start now. Retraining money, protections for workers, and a say for unions in how it rolls out. I'd keep saying it in tribunals, in the newsletter, everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a career, honestly. I could stay at Hale Brennan, become a partner by thirty-two, and pay off the car and help my sister finish. I'd only have to decide what's next in my mid-thirties, and that's a normal time to change direction anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and pick up the AI tools as they prove themselves at other firms. I'd push to become a partner in five years, and save properly once my sister graduates. I'd keep the paramedic idea in a drawer and look at it again in 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. My job looks safe for the next few years, and it would get busier. The worry is out there, somewhere in my thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be a lawyer in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, and maybe a partner, which would surprise my dad. Whether there are lawyers in 2040 is a different question. I'd be forty then, which is a good age to start something new if I had some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a law student today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a law student to learn to stand up in a room and argue, because that's the bit people still want from a person. And I'd tell them not to take on more debt than they could pay back in ten years. That's the honest truth.

say: **Ten years** is enough to do this properly if governments **start now**.
Unions need a **say** in how AI rolls out.
think: Ten years is a **whole career**, including a shot at partner by thirty-two.
I'd only need to decide what's next in my **mid-thirties**.
do: Push to become a **partner** within five years.
Pick up AI tools **once proven** at other firms.
feel: **Uneasy but not frightened**, with the real worry pushed into his thirties.
S4.quote: Learn to stand up in a room and argue, because that's the bit people still want from a lawyer.
fieldNote: Ten years turns AGI into a **later problem** he can plan around.
His advice to students mixes **advocacy** with a warning about **debt**.
He'd adopt tools at the **steady pace** of other firms, not first.

steps.text: Work towards partner at Hale Brennan within five years
Adopt AI tools once other firms show they work
Save properly once his sister finishes university

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no savings, no time and a career that ends right after I built it. What would help is a proper tax on the AI firms that pays for retraining, so someone like me could switch to paramedic training without losing the flat. A union voice in how it rolls out would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about families. I'm helping pay my sister's rent, and I suspect half the people my age are holding someone up. When one of us falls, two people fall.

headlineQuote: I'm helping pay my sister's rent, and I suspect half the people my age are holding someone up. When one of us falls, two people fall.
portrait: Nikhil leads a **worker-side employment team** at a small port-town firm, working closely with a union.
He has **two weeks of savings**, a car loan, and helps pay his sister's rent.
He uses AI **now and then** for reading bundles but keeps it away from clients.
He moves from **uneasy** to **alarmed** as AGI comes faster, and plans retraining as a paramedic.
He blames **tech firms and governments** and wants taxes and union voice.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most: no savings, no time, a career ending early.
